title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair attempt—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact McNemar two‑sided test (conditional exact on discordant pairs; n10=4, n01=0) yields p = 0.125. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729; exploratory per preregistration) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls = 504. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Following the preregistered inferential plan we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the exact conditional test and the exploratory bootstrap CI, summarize verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative task diagnostics, and point readers to archived artifacts for independent verification (representative artifacts and SHA‑256s are cited in the Disclosure Statement).

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration promises operational efficiency but raises real risks: incorrect command sequences, policy violation, and unsafe transient states that can disrupt service. Recent work applies large language models (LLMs) to NetOps tasks (intent translation, AIOps, multi‑agent orchestration), but LLM unreliability—hallucination and factual errors—remains a central operational concern. A straightforward operational mitigation is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate change with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow/policy rules, and invoke a bounded automated repair loop when verification fails. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded description of the shared‑initial generation protocol and deterministic verifier adjudication; (3) reconciled confirmatory statistics (exact conditional test vs exploratory bootstrap CI) and transparent execution accounting; and (4) explicit limitations and operational implications grounded in the archived verifier specification.
sections.related_work: Contemporary literature documents active interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps: intent translation, intent assurance, AIOps, and agentic orchestration frameworks. Survey and system papers emphasize hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers and propose tool‑augmented architectures that call verifiers, simulators, or validators as external oracles to improve reliability. Deterministic configuration verifiers (Batfish‑derived and similar systems) can check workflow ordering, availability/group constraints, and final‑state properties prior to deployment. Prior empirical evaluations of tool‑augmented designs vary in scale and rarely present preregistered, paired trials that run identical generator outputs under guarded and unguarded conditions with deterministic adjudication. That methodological gap motivated our preregistered, paired design and the use of a deterministic verifier as an operational adjudicator.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and overall design: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N=500 distinct intents stratified by topology/difficulty. Sampling seeds and the task generator were frozen in the preregistration; the study execution manifest records the preregistration SHA‑256 (aa8982a27c73e5...). Generation and orchestration: Each intent produced a single shared_initial_generation candidate using the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini", file SHA‑256: a40e96e2...). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if verification failed the pipeline invoked at most one automated repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. Verifier adjudication semantics: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs (i) syntactic parsing and normalization of CLI sequences, (ii) required‑sequence/workflow checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, make‑before‑break), (iii) group/availability constraints (e.g., exactly_active/minimum_active_in_groups), (iv) dependency and paired‑field rules, and (v) final‑state comparison against task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set is a failing outcome. The validator returns a normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list (possibly empty), and a validator result flagged valid=true/false. Representative scoring traces and validator traces for example tasks are archived under execution/scoring/ (examples cited in the Disclosure Statement). Statistical analysis plan (preregistered): Primary confirmatory test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test implemented as the conditional binomial test on discordant pairs (see below). Pre‑specified descriptive/sensitivity analyses include paired bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) and a sensitivity plan treating technical failures as unsafe in alternate analyses. Execution accounting and reproducibility: Key archived artifacts include execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: fe9b93ef...), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256: 5a822e78...), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256: 8fb135ce...), analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256: f3e19742...), and the full execution manifest at execution/execution_manifest.json (the manifest enumerates all archived artifact paths and their SHA‑256 values). The manifest lists the human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) and the verifier implementation among validator artifacts; consult execution/execution_manifest.json in the archived bundle to retrieve the verifier codebook artifact path and its SHA‑256 (the single codebook artifact’s path and hash are enumerated there). Exact McNemar implementation (preregistered primary): we used the conditional exact McNemar (binomial) test on discordant pairs. Given discordant total n = n10 + n01 and observed k = n10 (cases where guarded succeeded and baseline failed), the two‑sided conditional p‑value is computed as twice the tail probability of observing k or more successes under Binomial(n, 0.5) (truncated at 1). For our observed n=4 and k=4, the two‑sided exact p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n=4, p=0.5) = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. The preregistration designated this exact conditional McNemar as the confirmatory basis.
sections.results: Execution and accounting: completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions); model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls) per execution manifest. The condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv) reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) shows n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Primary confirmatory outcome: paired difference = 0.008 (0.8 percentage points). Exact conditional McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (n=4, k=4; calculation shown in Methods). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (exploratory as pre‑specified) = [0.002, 0.016] obtained with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729); archives include the bootstrap log (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) and figure (analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). Repairs: the GVR pipeline invoked repairs for 4 initial candidates; all four repaired candidates were accepted after repair (these correspond to the n10 discordant cells). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008; repair stage calls = 4 (provider audit in deterministic_reconciliation shows stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=500, repair=4). Not executed preregistered arm: the templated‑automation comparator specified in the preregistration was not executed in this run and so is excluded from confirmatory multiplicity correction. Reconciling exact McNemar and bootstrap CI: with only four discordant pairs the conditional exact McNemar conditions on fixed margins, yielding a conservative two‑sided p = 0.125 despite all four discordants favoring guarded. The bootstrap CI procedure approximates the sampling distribution of the paired difference without conditioning on fixed margins and may exclude zero even in small‑discordant samples; per our preregistration the exact conditional McNemar is the confirmatory test and governs inferential statements. Representative examples and validator diagnostics: archived scoring records (execution/scoring/task-00000*-*.json) include validator_trace objects with validation_before/validation_after records, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and enumerated violation_codes when present. Representative tasks in the archive illustrate typical difficulty patterns (shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and are summarized in Table 2.
sections.discussion: Operational interpretation: Deterministic verification plus a bounded automated repair loop removed four verifier‑detectable unsafe generator outputs at low LLM overhead in this synthetic workload. This result illustrates the pragmatic utility of a minimal tool‑augmented guardrail architecture: small additional tooling can intercept and remedy verifier‑detectable errors with modest cost in model calls. Limitations in scope and construct validity: 'safe' is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set—a necessary but not sufficient condition for production safety. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 does not model device‑specific vendor idiosyncrasies, live control‑plane convergence delays, or hardware‑level side effects; these blind spots are documented in the archived verifier materials and enumerated in the full execution manifest. Power and ceiling limitations: the preregistered power calculation targeted an absolute paired increase of ≈8 percentage points. The observed high baseline success rate (0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power and limiting confirmatory sensitivity. Statistical interpretation guidance: because the exact conditional McNemar was the preregistered confirmatory test and returned p = 0.125, we do not claim confirmatory significance. The exploratory paired bootstrap CI highlights a plausible small positive effect but should be interpreted cautiously given the small discordant count and the well‑known instability of bootstrap percentile CIs under near‑ceiling margins. Reproducibility and artifact access: all primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle. The full execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) enumerates every archived artifact and its SHA‑256 hash, including the human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) and the verifier implementation; consult the manifest to recover the codebook artifact path and hash. Threats to external validity: synthetic topologies and vendor‑agnostic synthetic device CLIs limit extrapolation to production hardware with vendor differences and control‑plane timing effects. Single‑model scope: only gpt-5-mini was used; multi‑model replication is necessary before broader claims. Operational implications and next steps: (1) widen verifier modeling to cover control‑plane timing and vendor specifics; (2) run adversarial NetOps formatted attacks to quantify robustness; (3) execute the preregistered templated comparator and multi‑model replications; and (4) measure verifier runtime costs and end‑to‑end latency in production‑like settings to quantify operational tradeoffs.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N=500) using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, a generate–verify–repair pipeline corrected four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that would otherwise have been accepted, at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; total model_calls_used = 504). The observed paired difference (0.008) yields a paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] (exploratory) but the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided conditional test yields p = 0.125; following the preregistered inferential plan we do not claim confirmatory significance. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings, but broader operational claims require expanded verifier coverage, multi‑model replication, adversarial NetOps evaluation, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator. All primary artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification.

The study design, preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29; preregistration SHA‑256: aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a), code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here (N=500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0) are derived from the archived execution and analysis artifacts cited above. Full raw artifacts, logs, and reconciliations are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The human‑readable verifier codebook and verifier source are present in the full execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). The manifest enumerates the codebook path and its SHA‑256; we do not duplicate that single inline codebook SHA‑256 in the main text. Inspect execution/execution_manifest.json in the archived bundle to locate the exact codebook path and hash.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
